intro: Four sample problems show the types of exam questions: a calculation, a graph drawn from data, an explanation and the planning of an experiment. Solve first yourself, then assess your answer with the model answer and the marking scheme.

tasks.title: Cycling up a hill
tasks.source_note: The numbers are chosen to be realistic, but they are not a measurement.
tasks.text: A cyclist rides up a road to the top of a hill. The total mass of the cyclist and the bicycle is $82.0\,\text{kg}$. The road is $1.20\,\text{km}$ long, and along it the height increases by $45.0\,\text{m}$. The cyclist's sports watch shows that the climb takes $4\,\text{min}\ 30\,\text{s}$, and the speed stays about the same for the whole climb. Air resistance and the rolling resistance of the tyres oppose the motion with a total average force of $18\,\text{N}$. The efficiency of the muscles is about $22\,\%$: that is the share of the energy from food that becomes work turning the pedals.

parts.text: How much does the potential energy of the cyclist and the bicycle increase during the climb?

criteria.detail: $\Delta E_\text{p} = mgh$, zero level at the bottom of the road.
$\Delta E_\text{p} \approx 36.2\,\text{kJ}$, three significant figures.

parts.text: How large an average power is needed just to lift the cyclist and the bicycle up the hill?

criteria.detail: $P = \dfrac{\Delta E_\text{p}}{t}$
The time in seconds $t = 270\,\text{s}$; $P \approx 134\,\text{W}$.

parts.text: How large a mechanical power must the cyclist produce on average during the climb?

criteria.text: The work of the muscles covers both the increase in potential energy and the work of the resistive forces; the kinetic energy does not change, because the speed is constant.

criteria.detail: The work of the resistive forces $W_\text{r} = F_\text{r} s = 21.6\,\text{kJ}$.
$P \approx 210\,\text{W}$, two significant figures like the force $18\,\text{N}$.

parts.text: How much energy from food does the climb use? Answer in kilojoules.

criteria.detail: $\eta = \dfrac{W}{E}$, so $E = \dfrac{W}{\eta}$
The energy from food is larger than the mechanical work, because the efficiency is below one.

parts.text: The cyclist's friend says that after the climb you can eat a bar of chocolate whose energy content is $2200\,\text{kJ}$ according to the wrapper, because the climb uses it up. Assess the claim.

criteria.text: The answer compares the numbers: the climb uses about $12\,\%$ of the energy of the bar, so the energy of the bar equals about eight climbs.

criteria.detail: The assumptions of the model: constant speed, an average resistive force and the efficiency of the muscles; the resting metabolism is not included.
The claim is not true: one climb uses only a small part of the energy of the bar.

tasks.title: The pendulum and the free-fall acceleration
tasks.source_note: The data have variation like that of a measurement, but they are not a measurement.
tasks.text:
Students hang a spherical bob from a thin string and measure the length $L$ of the string with a tape measure from the point of suspension to the top of the bob. The bob is pulled aside only a little, and the time $t_{10}$ of ten periods is measured with a stopwatch. The measurement is made with six lengths of string.

| $L\ (\text{m})$ | $t_{10}\ (\text{s})$ |
|---|---|
| $0.200$ | $9.33$ |
| $0.350$ | $12.08$ |
| $0.500$ | $14.42$ |
| $0.650$ | $16.41$ |
| $0.800$ | $18.08$ |
| $0.950$ | $19.72$ |

parts.text: Why do the students measure the time of ten periods and not of one?

criteria.detail: In hand timing the starting and stopping of the watch are late or early by about $0.2\,\text{s}$, which is a large part of the time of one period.
The same timing uncertainty is shared by ten periods, so the relative uncertainty of the period is a tenth.

parts.text: Make a graph of the data whose points lie on a straight line, and fit a line to it.

criteria.text: Chooses the quantities $L$ and $T^2$ for the axes and justifies the choice with the expression for the period of a pendulum $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}}$.

criteria.detail: The periods are calculated as $T = \tfrac{t_{10}}{10}$ and squared.
A straight line not forced through the origin is fitted to the points.

parts.text: Determine the free-fall acceleration from the graph.

criteria.detail: The slope read from the line at two points far apart: $k \approx 4.03\,\tfrac{\text{s}^2}{\text{m}}$.
$k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}$, so $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}$
$g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ or $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$, the unit derived from the unit of the slope.
The result is compared with the value $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

parts.text: The fitted line does not pass through the origin. Explain why, and assess whether it affects the result of part c.

criteria.detail: The line crosses the $L$ axis at about $L \approx -1.5\,\text{cm}$, that is it passes the vertical axis at about $0.06\,\text{s}^2$.
The length of the pendulum is from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob, but $L$ was measured to the top: every length is too short by the radius of the bob. The error is systematic.
A constant error shifts the line but does not change its slope, so $g$ from the slope is reliable; $g$ calculated from single points would be too small.

tasks.title: The vacuum flask
tasks.source_note: The numbers are chosen to be realistic, but they are not a measurement.
tasks.text: A vacuum flask has two glass walls, one inside the other. The air between the walls has been removed, and the surfaces of the walls facing each other are silvered like a mirror. The mouth of the flask has a stopper. In the morning a hiker pours $0.50\,\text{kg}$ of tea at $85.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ into the flask and closes the stopper. Six hours later, at $13.00$, the temperature of the tea is $70.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The outdoor temperature is about $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ the whole time. The specific heat capacity of the tea is the same as that of water, $4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$.

parts.text: Explain how the structure of the flask slows down the cooling of the tea. Deal with every way in which heat can be transferred.

criteria.text: Conduction: a vacuum has no particles to transfer energy by collisions from one wall to the other.
Convection: a vacuum has no air that could flow and carry energy.
Thermal radiation: the mirror surface reflects most of the thermal radiation from the side of the tea back.
The stopper stops the flow of steam and warm air at the mouth and the evaporation that would take up energy.

criteria.detail: There is still a net transfer of energy from the tea to the surroundings, but it is slow, for example through the mouth and the joint of the walls.

parts.text: The hiker notices that the tea cools more slowly in the afternoon than in the morning. Explain the observation.

criteria.text: The heat flow from the tea to the surroundings grows as the temperature difference between the tea and the surroundings grows.

criteria.detail: As the tea cools, the temperature difference decreases, so the heat flow and the rate of cooling decrease.

parts.text: Calculate the average heat flow with which energy is transferred from the tea to the surroundings during the six hours.

criteria.detail: $Q = cm\Delta T$ and $P = \dfrac{Q}{t}$
$t = 6.0 \cdot 3600\,\text{s}$; $P \approx 1.5\,\text{W}$, two significant figures.

parts.text: Does the vacuum flask also keep ice water cold? Justify your answer.

criteria.text: The same structures slow down the transfer of energy in both directions; now there is a net transfer of energy from the warm surroundings to the cold water.

criteria.detail: The comparison is fair when the temperature difference is about the same; in addition the melting of the ice takes up energy, so the water stays at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ as long as there is ice.
Yes: the vacuum flask also keeps a cold drink cold.

tasks.title: The efficiency of a kettle
tasks.source_note: The measured result of part b is chosen to be realistic, but it is not a measurement.
tasks.text: A group of students wants to find out whether the efficiency of a kettle depends on how much water is heated in it. They have a kettle with a power of $2.0\,\text{kW}$, a digital thermometer, kitchen scales, a stopwatch, tap water and an energy meter connected between the socket and the kettle, which shows the electrical energy used to $0.001\,\text{kWh}$. Only the warming of the water counts as useful.

parts.text: Plan an experiment with which the group can find out.

criteria.text: The quantity changed is the mass of the water, for example five different amounts from the smallest mark of the kettle to the largest.
Kept constant: the same kettle, the same initial and final temperature, the lid closed and the kettle cooled to room temperature between the measurements.
Measured: the mass of the water with the scales, the initial and final temperature with the thermometer and the electrical energy used with the energy meter.
Every measurement is repeated, for example three times, and the mean of the results is calculated.
The plan goes step by step so clearly that another group could repeat it.

parts.text: In one measurement the kettle holds $0.500\,\text{kg}$ of water, which warms from $15.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $95.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and the energy meter shows $0.054\,\text{kWh}$. Calculate the efficiency of the kettle.

criteria.detail: $\eta = \dfrac{Q}{E}$, where $Q = cm\Delta T$
$\eta \approx 86\,\%$, two significant figures like the reading $0.054\,\text{kWh}$.
The efficiency is below $100\,\%$; the rest of the energy heats the kettle and the surroundings.

parts.text: Assess the sources of error of the experiment and say how their effect can be reduced.

criteria.detail: For example, water evaporates while it is heated, the kettle is warm from the previous measurement and the thermometer measures at one point only.
The reading of the energy meter to $0.001\,\text{kWh}$ is about $2\,\%$ of the reading $0.054\,\text{kWh}$ and an even larger share with small amounts of water.

criteria.text: Suggests measures: the lid closed, the kettle cooled, the water stirred before the reading and the measurements repeated.

parts.text: How does the group present the results, and what kind of result would show that the efficiency depends on the amount of water?

criteria.detail: An $(m, \eta)$ graph: the mass of the water $m\ (\text{kg})$ on the horizontal axis and the efficiency $\eta\ (\%)$ on the vertical axis.
A dependence is shown only if the change in efficiency is clearly larger than the scatter of the repeats.
For example, the efficiency grows as the amount of water grows, because the energy used to heat the body of the kettle is a smaller part of the whole.
